newsitem.title: CROATIA: Talks with Tudjman advance Serb-Croat relations.
newsitem.headline: Talks with Tudjman advance Serb-Croat relations.

text.p: A U.N. mandate to restore Croatian government rule over a breakaway Serb enclave peacefully received a boost on Saturday when local Serb leaders met President Franjo Tudjman for the first time.

U.N., Croatian and Serb officials described the two hours of talks between Tudjman and the nine-member Serb delegation from Eastern Slavonia as constructive and a hopeful sign of Serbo-Croatian rapprochement.
Serb forces seized almost a third of Croatia in a 1991 revolt against the government's move to independence, touching off the bloody disintegration of multinational Yugoslavia.

Croatia retook two of three Serb pockets in counter-attacks last year, then accepted a U.N. mission (UNTAES) to gradually "reintegrate" Eastern Slavonia, averting further war that could have unhinged the new peace in nearby Bosnia.

On Wednesday, the nationalist Croatian government, in a conciliatory gesture, agreed in principle to a six-month extension of the United Nations' mandate to July 1997 recommended by senior U.N. officials.

That would give transitional U.N. administrators more time to foster Serbo-Croat reconciliation at the grassroots level, defusing fears of local Serbs that they would be stampeded out by vengeful returning Croats.

At his presidential palace, Tudjman met U.N. mission chief Jacques Klein, local Serb executive council president Vojislav Stanimirovic and aides responsible for human rights issues, education, agriculture, justice and other concerns.
Stanimirovic referred to Tudjman as "the president", a far cry from separatist Serb terminology of the recent past, and described Croatia's laws on minority rights as "positive".

In remarks after the meeting, Stanimirovic welcomed Croatia's admission to the Council of Europe, antechamber of the European Union, a few days before and said this would promote satisfactory solutions for Serbs in Croatia.

He said a few key issues remained unresolved, including his community's demand that all local Serbs, not just original 1991 residents, be able to vote in regional elections to be held just before 5,000 U.N. troops withdraw.
"We hope elections will be possible in March 1997," he said. That timetable corresponds to the government's.

The Serbs, whose militia army was disarmed by UNTAES last summer, also want "soft borders" to foster free travel and trade with neighbouring rump Yugoslavia, and exemption from service in the Croatian army.

Roughly 120,000 Serbs, possibly one half or more of them refugees from reconquered enclaves, are believed to live in Eastern Slavonia, a fertile and oil-rich plain skirting the Danube River border with Serbia.
In another symbolic step forward, Tudjman met a delegation of the Serbian Orthodox Church last week for the first time since independence.
Tudjman, 74, an authoritarian former general long accused of trampling on minority rights, used striking words of reconciliation tailored for European Union consumption in a speech early this month.
"Let us be prudent and broadminded and show it is not in our interest to see Serbs leave (Eastern Slavonia)," he said.
